subject: Recap + next steps: performance targets & scale priming (AtlasHealth)
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Sam Taylor <sam.taylor@atlashealth.com>, Priya Nair <priya.nair@atlashealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 2 Nov 2026 14:12:00 -0700
Subject: Recap + next steps: performance targets & scale priming (AtlasHealth)

Thanks again for the call this morning — good conversation and clear priorities. Summarizing what we heard and proposed next steps so we have a single place to track.

Key customer goals (as stated):
- 95th pct latency target for inference end-to-end: <= 300ms for single-shot text generation (non-streaming)
- Streaming use case: token-stream latency under 150ms per first-byte for 90% of sessions; overall session TTFB priority
- Sustained throughput target: 500 concurrent active requests (mixed text/gen + embeddings)
- Burst requirement: ability to absorb spikes up to ~2,000 concurrent requests for short windows (1–3 minutes) with degraded but acceptable latencies
- Recovery/scale-up expectation: from cold baseline to burst-capable within ~90 seconds; warm pool to reduce cold starts
- Queueing behavior: customer tolerates short queuing (<30s at 99th) with explicit backpressure; prefer queue admission control over dropping

What Redwood proposes / clarifications:
- Warm pool sizing: recommend starting with 20–30 prewarmed instances (we matched initial estimate to your 2k burst for 90s ramp). We will run a calibration test to refine.
- Autoscale ramp: default policy we discussed is aggressive ramp with step concurrency + continuous batching; we can provision a fast-path that scales to 60% capacity in ~45s and full burst reach in ~90s in the region you indicated.
- Streaming specifics: we will route streaming sessions to prewarmed nodes where possible; fallback to non-streaming nodes only if capacity constrained (we'll surface partial tokens).
- Queueing SLA: we propose an admission policy that keeps 95th latency in target by placing excess traffic in a capped queue; we'll expose metrics and an instrumented retry header for your client.

Immediate next steps (owners & ETA):
- Atlas: share internal load profile + any synthetic scripts (Sam / Priya) — ETA: Wed, Nov 4
- Redwood: provide test harness + initial warm-pool recommendation based on your load profile (Ben) — ETA: Thu, Nov 5
- Joint: schedule technical verification run (30–45m) to validate scale-up & streaming behavior (Ben / Marissa) — propose Nov 6 or Nov 9

Attachments: atlas-load-test-specs.pdf (you referenced this during call) — please upload the final version or confirm the test scenarios. I've attached a draft mutual action plan (atlas-mutual-action-plan.xlsx) for review.

Questions for you:
1) For streaming, is first-byte latency for interactive typing or long-running token streams? (affects caching strategy)
2) Are there hard SLAs for tail latency where you'd want active fallbacks or circuit breakers?

Thanks — happy to iterate.

—
Ben Carter
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0183

From: Sam Taylor <sam.taylor@atlashealth.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Nair <priya.nair@atlashealth.com>
Date: Tue, 3 Nov 2026 08:27:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Recap + next steps: performance targets & scale priming (AtlasHealth)

Thanks Ben — this is helpful and captures the priorities. Quick answers:
- Streaming is primarily interactive typing for clinicians (short sessions, bursty typing) rather than long continuous generation. First-byte latency is most important for user-perceived responsiveness.
- We do not have contractual tail-latency SLAs today, but operations will escalate if 99th exceeds ~3s. So having a deterministic queueing/backpressure behavior is more important than entirely eliminating queues.

We will circulate our internal load profile (Priya will attach earlier today) and include the synthetic scripts we use for peak-hour simulations.

For the technical verification run: Nov 9 at 10:00am PT works better on our side. Please include the runtime engineer who can tweak autoscale policies during the test.

Sam
Director of Engineering, AtlasHealth
sam.taylor@atlashealth.com

Date: Thu, 5 Nov 2026 09:42:00 -0700
Subject: Confirmed: tech verification run (Nov 9) + what we'll bring

Sam / Priya — great, Nov 9 10:00am PT is confirmed on our side. Agenda for the 45-minute technical verification run:
- 10m: test plan review & roles (who triggers what)
- 20m: run phased load (incremental concurrency -> sustained -> spike) while we monitor routing, queueing, and prewarm behavior
- 10m: tune autoscale policy (warm pool size, step sizes) and run 1 targeted spike to observe ramp behavior
- 5m: next steps + action items

What Redwood will provide during the run:
- Live dashboards (latency percentiles, queue depth, autoscale events, prewarm occupancy)
- Canary model variant to isolate impact of quantization changes (Rishi will own)
- A minimal runbook for client-side retry/backoff headers (I attached a draft in the mutual action plan)

Ask before the run: please confirm the synthetic script name you want us to use (from the load profile) and whether you want token-stream-first-byte measurement as part of the run — we'll prioritize that if so.

Related resources: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1A2b3AtlasLoadTests (test specs + mock scripts), HubSpot: 1092837

Attachments during run: atlas-load-test-specs.pdf, atlas-mutual-action-plan.xlsx

Thanks — see you next week.
